answer.label: Reported in English as saying
answer.sourceLine: A contemporary TIME report prints these words as Nikita Khrushchev’s remarks to Western diplomats at the Polish Embassy reception in Moscow in November 1956. They are a reported English translation of Russian remarks.

source.heading: The source
source.excerpt: Whether you like it or not, history is on our side. We will bury you.
trail: TIME’s contemporary report ↗ prints both clauses in its account of the reception.
The historical reference ↗ discusses subsequent explanations of the burial metaphor. The line should not be moved to a later United Nations speech.
source.rightsNote: The English wording checked is a contemporary 1956 magazine report. It is treated as copyrighted; only the short phrase is reproduced.

author.name: Nikita Khrushchev
author.heading: About Nikita Khrushchev
author.bio: Nikita Khrushchev led the Soviet Communist Party after Stalin and also served as Soviet premier. His period in power combined de-Stalinization with intense Cold War confrontations, including the Berlin and Cuban missile crises.

cite.sourceCitation: “Foreign News: We Will Bury You!” TIME, 26 November 1956. Reported English rendering of Khrushchev’s November reception remarks.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: The remark appeared amid sharp exchanges over the Soviet bloc and Western policy during the 1956 crises. Later explanations framed burial as capitalism’s historical defeat rather than a promise of physical destruction; the reported phrase and its intended meaning are separate historical questions.
